body_markdown:
Sheer, unbridled excitement.


That’s what the designers at Stellantis’ Turin studio must have felt the moment they heard that the powers that be would finally let them sculpt a proper Alfa Romeo.


With the Cuorerosso concept, unveiled at this year’s Paris Auto Show, Alfa Romeo reminded us that it hadn’t forgotten its history. This time around, there’d be no more tarting up Jeep Compasses or small Peugeots to make yet another forgettable crossover. No more compromises, no more excuses. I wish I could be a fly on the wall that day, just to sense the energy building in the room and to witness that creative rush that makes entire weeks fly by like hours.


Stellantis


I’m saying this because, as a former car designer now working in design education, I can tell you for a fact that the professionals in an automaker’s studio are just like us: hardcore gearheads with, as General Motors’ legendary Bill Mitchell famously put it, “gasoline in their veins.”


Stellantis


So it shouldn’t surprise you that a bright red Alfa is the kind of assignment pretty much every designer worth his salt dreams of. It’s always there, either in the back of their mind or tucked away in their portfolio, and they hope one day they’ll get to do it for real. Now that the guys at the Alfa Romeo studio in Turin have finally been handed the chance of a lifetime, what did they do with it? Does their work measure up to the Scagliones, Giugiaros, and Gandinis of this world?


Well, the initial consensus seems pretty positive, and again—it’s no surprise. After all, a cherry red Alfa is a vehicle enthusiasts are hardwired to embrace. Still, to try and answer the loaded question I posed above more professionally, I’ll break down the Cuorerosso’s design into its basic elements, starting with the fundamentals: stance and proportions.


Stellantis


Stellantis


Stellantis


Stellantis


To maximize visual impact, Alfa’s designers have gone all in, giving their new baby proportions that would make a Hot Wheels car blush. For starters, the Cuorerosso sits on four chunky 22-inch wheels, but its roofline tops out at just over 4 feet. Overall length is a fairly compact 15.5 feet, but the cabin stretches over a nearly 10-foot wheelbase, pushing the large wheels to the extremities and keeping the overhangs relatively short. The low, swooping bonnet line, coupled with the steeply raked windscreen and the tall, stubby rear end, creates a dramatic wedge shape that makes the Cuorerosso look like it’s doing 150 even as it’s sitting on a turntable. So far, so very, very good indeed.


[Bryan Gerould](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bryan-gerould/)


After proportion comes the sculpture, and I have to say that, for the most part, the *équipe* guided by Alejandro Mesonero-Romanos has done a fine job. The Cuorerosso’s surfaces are voluptuous and organic, yet they always retain a tension that gives the whole car a sense of restrained power, like a beast ready to pounce. In that sense, the Cuorerosso reminds me a lot of Mazda’s best work on its[recent concept cars](https://www.hagerty.com/media/design/mazda-iconic-sp-concept-2023-design-analysis-miata-future/) , and I really mean that as a compliment. If I had to pinpoint one part that really bugs me, though, it’s the awkward “beak” on the lower rear end, which I find a bit clumsy, and the graphic elements in that area only seem to emphasize that feeling. More on that in a moment.


Stellantis


Stellantis


Stellantis


Stellantis


Now, car designers generally use the term “graphics” as an umbrella term for all the lines that “cut” into a vehicle’s volume, from the contours of the headlights and windows to the air intake and the shutlines of the doors. Again, the Alfa designers seem to have done a fine job here, too. The side windows that cut into the roof remind me of[Zagato’s “Panoramica” bodies from the late 1940s](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/celebrating-100-years-of-zagato/) , but the result here is much easier on the eye. I wish the classic Alfa “Trilobo” graphic at the front had been treated more creatively, but as I mentioned earlier, the only real problem I see with the Cuorerosso is at the back.


Stellantis


I have no trouble with the tall rear-end surface, which is also Zagato-esque, or the taillight design, redolent of the latest 33 Stradale. Those frowny round “eyes” sit perfectly well there, but then there’s that aforementioned “beak” at bumper level and the wide opening sitting just below it. In this context, placing a large single exhaust outlet in the center seems like an especially poor decision: The whole composition, at least to my eye, ends up giving the Cuorerosso’s rear end the expression of an angry Pokémon. How anyone could miss this during the design phase is, frankly, beyond me.


Last, but definitely not least, I must mention the absolutely stunning design of the forged alloy wheels. Not only is it a thoughtful reinterpretation of the classic “teledial” design so beloved by Alfa fans, but its almost jewel-like intricacy makes the Cuorerosso’s wheels a joy to behold, at least until someone needs to scrub brake dust off them!


Stellantis


In typical concept-car fashion, the Cuorerosso’s cabin has no center pillar, and the four doors open wide for an unobstructed view of the interior, which is refreshingly free of touchscreens. I’m particularly fond of the steering wheel design, a clever homage to the three-spoke wheels of[1960s Alfas](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/your-handy-1967-77-alfa-romeo-gtv-buyers-guide/) , with their horn buttons integrated into the spokes. The only screens are those in the instrument binnacle, which again delights us with a well-thought-out, very contemporary take on a classic Alfa Romeo styling trope.


Stellantis


Even though it’s unlikely that this concept will reach production as-is, the Cuorerosso is nevertheless a welcome sign of life from a beloved brand that seems perennially stuck in a painful “one step ahead, two steps back” holding pattern. Come November, it’ll be 40 years since a heavily indebted, failing Alfa Romeo left the cold, dead hand of state ownership to join what was then known as Fiat Auto. I was only four years old then, which means I’ve heard managers plead for Alfa’s return to greatness for as long as I’ve been alive.


Still, I really hope the Cuorerosso will be a turning point for Alfa Romeo because, while I’m certainly not holding my breath, I’d still love to see this storied Italian name live up to its illustrious, heroic heritage before my days are over.


Sato Ficili, CEO of Alfa Romeo & Maserati

*Matteo Licata received his degree in Transportation Design from Turin’s IED (Istituto Europeo di Design) in 2006. He worked as an automobile designer for about a decade, including a stint in the then-Fiat Group’s Turin design studio, during which his proposal for the interior of the 2010–20 Alfa Romeo Giulietta was selected for production. He next joined Changan’s European design studio in Turin and then EDAG in Barcelona, Spain. Licata currently teaches automobile design history to the Transportation Design bachelor students of IAAD (Istituto di Arte Applicata e Design) in Turin.*
